context_blurb:
Some changes only reshape a thing: ice melts, paper tears, a rock is crushed to dust. Others make something brand new. That is a chemical change, or chemical reaction: atoms, the tiny building blocks of all matter, rearrange into a new substance with new properties. Atoms are far too small to watch, so scientists look for clues.

A physical change alters only a thing's shape, size or state (solid, liquid or gas) and makes nothing new. The signs of a chemical change are a gas given off, a change in temperature, a solid appearing in a liquid, a new colour, light and a new smell. Each sign is a clue, not proof, since physical changes can show some too.

Take bubbles. Drop an antacid tablet into cool water and, once it is wet, two of its ingredients react and make carbon dioxide, a gas that was not there before. Boiling water bubbles hard too, but its bubbles are only water turned into a gas. Of the two, only the bubbles from the tablet hold a new substance, since boiling is a change of state that makes nothing new.

A change in temperature is another clue. A hand warmer is a cloth pouch of damp iron powder and salt, sealed in an airtight wrapper. Open the wrapper and oxygen from the air reaches the iron. Rusting is a chemical change that gives off heat, and the salt speeds it up, so the iron rusting very fast is what heats the pouch. An iron gate rusts too slowly for its heat to be felt; powder, with far more iron touching the air, rusts fast.

A burning log gives off heat, but some reactions take in heat instead. Stirred together in a flask, two white powders, barium hydroxide and ammonium chloride, react into new substances, ammonia gas among them. The reaction draws heat from everything around it, so the flask drops to about twenty degrees Celsius below zero and freezes a wet wooden block to its glass. Cold is not a thing that flows out of the powders: the flask feels cold because heat is leaving whatever touches it.

A third clue is a precipitate, a solid that appears in a liquid. Limewater is clear water with lime, a chemical called calcium hydroxide, dissolved in it. Blow into it through a straw and it soon turns milky. The carbon dioxide in your breath reacts with the lime and makes calcium carbonate, the white stuff of chalk and limestone, which does not dissolve. Its tiny grains of solid hang in the liquid and turn it white.

A new colour can be a clue too. Shiny reddish-orange copper, left on a roof in rain and wind for years, turns pale blue-green. The green comes from the copper reacting with air and rain: oxygen, carbon dioxide and water slowly combine with it into a crust called a patina, a new substance with its own colour. The patina shields the metal beneath, so a copper roof can last more than a hundred years.

Yet colour can fool you. Shiny, steel-grey hematite, rubbed across an unglazed white tile, leaves a reddish-brown powder. That powder is the same mineral, ground very fine: rubbing only breaks the hematite into tiny grains, a physical change that makes nothing new. Many minerals give a powder of a different colour from the lump; geologists call that colour the streak and use it to tell minerals apart. So a new colour alone is never proof.

Light can be a clue as well. Bending a glow stick snaps a thin glass vial inside, and shaking mixes the vial's liquid with the one around it. The two liquids react as they mix and give off light with very little heat, so the stick shines for hours with no battery. A glow-in-the-dark toy only soaks up light and gives it back slowly; a glow stick needs no light first.

Last comes a new smell. Fresh sweat, mostly water with a little salt and fat, hardly smells at all. Bacteria living on the skin feed on sweat and break it down into new, smelly substances, which is why a runner's shirt reeks at the armpits after a long, hot race.
